title: Nepal’s rhino census is getting a scientific makeover - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal’s rhino census is getting a scientific makeover  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal is preparing to overhaul the way it counts its one-horned rhinos, moving away from a decades-old system that sends people into the jungle on elephants to spot and record the conserved animals.

The move comes as Nepal seeks better data on a rhino population that has recovered from historic lows but continues to face significant threats.

Nepal’s rhino population has risen sharply since it fell to about 100 in the 1960s, but 133 rhinos have died in and around Chitwan National Park over the past five years.

Authorities say the existing counting method is risky for survey teams and does not produce the kind of scientific data now needed to manage the population.

The Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation is considering genetic sampling, camera traps or a combination of the two for the next census. A committee will first prepare a protocol and conduct pilot studies before recommending a methodology.

“The department is preparing to revise the old method and adopt a new one,” said Haribhadra Acharya, a senior ecologist at the department. “We will conduct pilot studies to develop the methodology.”

Nepal currently has 752 one-horned rhinos, according to department data. More than 92 percent of them live in Chitwan National Park, making the park the centre of the country’s rhino conservation effort.

The 2021 census counted 694 rhinos in Chitwan, 38 in Bardiya National Park, 17 in Shuklaphanta National Park and three in Parsa National Park.

The next census is normally due after four or five years, but authorities are now preparing to change how it is conducted.

For decades, survey teams have divided rhino habitat into blocks and moved through them on elephants, spotting and counting the animals directly. Under the so-called ‘sweep operation’, elephants carrying the surveyors are positioned close enough for one team to see another as they search their assigned areas.

The method has become increasingly difficult to defend.

About 40 elephants were deployed each day during previous counts, with two counters riding on each elephant. The animals had to work from morning until evening and could become tired and aggressive.

There was also the danger of encounters with wild elephants.

During the 2021 census, a male wild elephant encountered one of the elephants being used by the survey team. The elephant carrying the counters bolted, throwing and dragging a technician who was injured. He remains disabled, Acharya said.

“Risk is high, and it is also difficult to obtain the actual data,” he said.

The department also says the equipment used in previous counts was inadequate and that the technology was not sufficiently scientific or reliable.

That is prompting officials to look beyond the traditional approach. Camera traps are already used to estimate tiger populations, while rhinos have generally been counted through direct observation.

“Tiger numbers are determined digitally through camera trapping, whereas rhinos have been counted by people seeing them directly,” Acharya said. “The tiger census is therefore considered scientific, while the rhino census has mainly been aimed at finding out the number of animals.”

A recovery with continuing threats

The proposed change in census methodology comes against the backdrop of a remarkable but uneven recovery.

Nepal had about 800 rhinos in the 1950s. By the following decade, their numbers had collapsed to around 100. Conservation programmes subsequently helped the population recover, turning the one-horned rhino into one of the country’s most recognisable wildlife species.

But the animals continue to die from a range of causes.

Chitwan recorded 22 rhino deaths in the fiscal year 2025–26, including 20 inside the national park and two in the surrounding national forest. The park recorded 30 deaths in 2024–25, 21 in 2023–24, 23 in 2022–23 and 37 in 2021–22.

Rhinos die naturally as they age, but deaths also result from fights between animals, getting trapped in marshes and mud, electrocution and, occasionally, tiger attacks. Poaching remains a conservation concern, although no rhino has been killed by poachers in Chitwan since October 2023, according to park officials.

“Conservation has not produced the results we had hoped for because of habitat-management problems and the limited resources available,” said Abinash Thapa Magar, information officer and conservation officer at Chitwan National Park.

Human-rhino conflict is another problem. Rhinos sometimes enter agricultural land and damage crops, increasing tensions between communities and wildlife.

Thapa Magar said awareness campaigns, greater vigilance and tighter security had helped reduce poaching.

“We do not have any concrete evidence yet about where the horns of poached rhinos end up or what they are used for,” he said.

The department has a 2024–34 action plan for rhino conservation.

More than a tourist attraction

For Nepal, the stakes go beyond the survival of a charismatic animal.

The greater one-horned rhino is found only in parts of Nepal and India. Its horn can grow to between 20 and 100 centimetres, while its massive body, thick folds of skin and distinctive appearance make it a major draw for wildlife tourists.

Hundreds of thousands of visitors come to Nepal each year, and rhino sightings are an important part of the country’s wildlife tourism industry.

“The rhino is a flagship species of riverine areas, so its ecological importance is equally significant,” said Dr Naresh Subedi, a former member-secretary of the National Trust for Nature Conservation.

Rhinos also alter the environment around them. By feeding on large grasses, they help keep forests and grasslands open and create habitat for smaller animals. For that reason, conservationists refer to them as ‘ecosystem engineers’.

Their relationship with other wildlife is also significant, according to Dr Ghana Shyam Gurung, a WWF Nepal representative.

“Saving rhinos also helps save tigers, and vice versa, so the species has a distinct importance,” Gurung said. “Rhinos are prehistoric animals, which is another reason people are fascinated by them.”

For tourists, the appeal is simpler. Nature guide Dinesh Giri said visitors often take elephant-back or jeep safaris to watch rhinos moving through their natural habitat, their massive bodies swaying as they walk or wallow in mud.

The animals are generally peaceful when left alone. But that can change quickly when they feel threatened. A frightened or angry rhino can run at high speed and attack.

title: Opinion | How Nepal’s current crisis sparks a new vision for multilateral engagements in the face of climate challenges - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | How Nepal’s current crisis sparks a new vision for multilateral engagements in the face of climate challenges  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Has Nepal actively supported multilateralism in recent years? Is it now seeking global support for an unprecedented natural crisis through its most favoured and established diplomatic platform—multilateralism? Or are natural disasters themselves transforming Nepal’s diplomatic practices? Indeed, we need a more detailed and objective discussion of these self-critical questions before assessing the fragility of contemporary multilateralism and developing our diplomatic strategies.

It is fair to say that Nepal could not have fully escaped—more precisely, has not given sufficient attention to—the broader critical perception that Nepal often consumes most of its diplomatic energy responding to power games among a limited number of superpowers. As clearly illustrated in Nepal’s Foreign Policy 2020, the country pays particular attention to the changing nature and dynamics of the world order, particularly those shaped by shifts in the material power capabilities of the superpowers. It is also widely claimed and criticised that Nepal often alternates between external balancing and hedging—two primary strategies emphasised by material power-based theories of international relations—in its relations with the major powers. On the other hand, its overemphasis on political relations with a limited number of major powers has been interpreted as evidence of Nepal’s waning interest in multilateralism in recent years.

In this background, we must not underestimate the fact that Nepal’s position and strategies at the 81 st UN General Assembly could mark a turning point in Nepal’s diplomatic path. The international community will interpret our diplomatic interests, strategies and future direction through the words, language and positions we articulate. Our prime minister’s speech will also mark the return to Nepal’s normal diplomatic practice following the political upheaval of September 2025. Nepal and its prime minister will also receive unprecedented attention at this Assembly.

Hence, we must consider two responsibilities simultaneously: making a sincere and compelling appeal to the international community for its support to overcome the natural crisis, as well as reaffirming our commitment to multilateralism with a clear vision for its future. In fact, we must recognise that we have entered a phase of developing a new Nepali vision of multilateralism centred on the climate change crisis.

To develop this vision, we first need to establish a clear and shared understanding of the contemporary state of multilateralism—particularly the nature and causes of its fragility. As Robert Keohane, a prominent neoliberal institutionalist, defines it, multilateralism is “the practice of coordinating national policies in groups of three or more states, through ad hoc arrangements or by means of institutions.”

Not only is the quantitative prerequisite of the participation of more than three national governments important, but several qualitative dimensions of multilateralism are also globally emphasised. Among these, three are particularly significant. First and foremost, we cannot conceive of multilateralism without placing generalised principles of conduct at its centre. Political scientist John Ruggie defines this core principle as one that ‘specifies appropriate conduct for a class of actions, without regard to particularistic interests of the parties or strategic exigencies that may exist in any specific occurrence’. It therefore precludes ad hoc or arbitrary responses driven by the particular interests and circumstances of individual states. It is thus unsurprising that multilateralism embodies the universal ideals that have shaped the liberal international order in the post-war era.

Agreed indivisibility is the second key quality of multilateralism. The members of multilateral communities are expected to share the burden collectively. More precisely, this principle has roots in the idealism that was influential during the inter-war period. It assumes that states can formulate reciprocal policies by taking into account both their own national interests and those of others. Adherence to international norms ultimately benefits all member states and humanity as a whole. The third main principle is diffuse reciprocity. As political scientist James Caporaso states, members of multilateral arrangements ‘expect to benefit in the long run and over many issues, rather than every time on every issue’.

What are the key phenomena or issues that seriously challenge the practical application of these basic principles of multilateralism in the contemporary world? Several issues and agendas have already been widely highlighted in global debates. These include the rise of the nation-first principle; heated trade competition and the revival of protectionism; the growing use of negotiationism; direct negotiations among the leaders of key countries that bypass key bilateral and multilateral institutions—a natural practice in the era of populism; the weak performance of several intergovernmental organisations in managing conflicts among member states; and so forth.

Two fundamental and interconnected issues underpin the global discourse on the crisis of multilateralism. First and foremost, a lack of committed global leadership fails to uphold and carry forward traditions that have already proved effective, bring key disputes to the table, and initiate discussions aimed at resolving them. In fact, the absence of effective leadership in multilateralism is a key psychological factor underlying the persistent discourse of crisis. We are already witnessing a clear global polarity: strong demands from middle powers to revitalise multilateralism, contrasted with the largely normative commitments of the superpowers.

Second, the visible limitations of international organisations in addressing issues such as trade, human rights and the environment have raised questions about their effectiveness and, more broadly, the liberal international order. Questions about whether states can actually unite to resolve collective problems have come to dominate academic and public discourse, gradually influencing politics and policymaking as well.

title: Kathmandu Post Column Criticizes Nepal’s Government After Floods - UA.NEWS
description: Kathmandu Post Column Criticizes Nepal’s Government After Floods  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, the government of Prime Minister Balendra Shah creates an impression of control through digital communication and public gestures, while problems in public policy, the economy and disaster response remain unresolved. This assessment was expressed by the author of a Kathmandu Post column.

The columnist links this criticism to the aftermath of sudden floods in the Rasuwa district and nearby areas. The United States announced $500,000 in emergency aid for those affected, to be delivered through Catholic Relief Services.

Aid and climate risks

The column compares this amount with US aid after the 1954 monsoon floods, when Washington announced a package of approximately $2 million. The author considers the current support symbolic and links the scale of international aid to the strategic interests of donor states.

He also notes that Nepal’s share of global greenhouse gas emissions is less than 0.1%, yet the country is experiencing serious consequences of global warming. In the columnist’s view, calls for climate justice do not guarantee substantial financial support from major polluting states.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Reconstruction and trip to the UN

The author writes that after the disaster on the Bhotekoshi, the rescue operation has not yet been completed, while assistance to those affected and reconstruction will require time. According to his description, the water washed away many facilities, from local government bodies to police posts.

According to the column, Balendra Shah is to make his first foreign trip after taking office to speak at the UN General Assembly in the United States. The columnist suggests that the prime minister will raise the issue of climate justice there.

Heavy rains were forecast in Nepal for September 24–28. The author warns that they could destabilize mountain slopes already saturated with moisture after the monsoon and make rivers more dangerous. He also criticizes the notion that political stability by itself guarantees prosperity and believes that the digital image of a decisive government does not replace systemic solutions.

title: Can Tenzing Sherpa save Nepal from an empty-handed karate campaign? - The Kathmandu Post
description: Can Tenzing Sherpa save Nepal from an empty-handed karate campaign?  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
One final chance remains for Nepal’s karate to make sure they do not have to return without a single medal from the 20 th Asian Games. Seven Nepali karatekas have been knocked out of their respective categories until Tuesday.

Tenzing Sherpa is the only player left from the eight-player contingent of Nepali karate. He is facing On Tek Leong of Macau, China, in the men’s kumite +84kg quarterfinals on Wednesday.

Karate has been one of the most successful sports for Nepal in the Asian Games, after taekwondo and boxing.

Sita Rai was the first to win a medal for karate—a bronze in the 1994 Asian Games in Hiroshima, Japan. Samar Bahadur Gole then bagged another bronze in karate in the 1998 Asian Games in Bangkok, Thailand.

It took a while for Nepal to win medals in karate again. In the 2014 Asian Games in Incheon, South Korea, Nepal won only a single medal—by karate’s Bimala Tamang. And it was in the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, which took place in 2023 due to Covid-19, when Nepal could announce that gold in karate was possible.

Arika Gurung won silver for Nepal in karate in Hangzhou. It was Nepal’s second silver in individual sports in the Asian Games after 25 years—the first coming from taekwondoin Sabita Rajbhandari in 1998 in Bangkok.

Nepal has won three silvers in the Asian Games so far. Alongside Rajbhandari and Gurung, the other silver was won by the paragliding team in the 2018 Asian Games in Indonesia.

Gurung was expected to bring gold in 2026 but she crashed out in the semi-final.

And when Nepal is struggling for a single medal in the ongoing 20 th edition in Nagoya, karate’s Sherpa has huge hopes and responsibility on his shoulders.

Nepal’s Arika Gurung is struck by Saudi Arabia’s Dina Ahmed S Mostafa during the women’s kumite +68kg bronze medal bout on Sunday. Photo: Courtesy of Asian Games

Statistically, Sherpa has an upper hand over Leong. The World Karate Federation (WKF) ranks Sherpa 139 th with 165 points and Leong 212 th with 55 points in the men’s kumite +84kg in the world.

However, this gap is only in the +84kg category. Leong has risen along the weight categories, having competed in the cadet -57kg and -63kg, junior -68kg, U21 -67kg, and male -75kg and -84kg all around the world, making him more experienced than Sherpa.

Meanwhile, Gurung getting knocked out without a medal in the ongoing tournament has shown that previous stats hardly matter.

Sanu Maya Thing, whose team was also expected to bring a medal, also got knocked out of the women’s individual kata Round of 16, alongside failing to reach the podium at the women’s team kata quarterfinals.

Megha Limbu and Alisa Raskoti Magar were in the women’s kata team alongside Thing. They lost the Round of 16 against South Korea and the quarterfinals against Vietnam, before losing the bronze medal show against Chinese Taipei.

“Nepal has a strong squad in team kata, and our performance today was our best so far,” said Manday Kaji Shrestha, coach of the Nepali kata team. “Despite that, being defeated makes not just me as a coach, but the entire Nepali team sad. We only began preparations for team kata two months prior to the Asian Games. We had high hopes but fell short of bringing home a medal today despite giving our best performance.”

Shrestha argued that it was not the end. “In the days ahead, we can deliver even better performances and win medals,” he said. “Looking back, we were quite behind in kata. After the Hangzhou Asiad three years ago, when the Nepal Karate Federation and the National Sports Council arranged international exposure, we reached our current level…If we focus on team kata preparations rather than individual events, we can win medals in the future.”

Similarly, Min Bahadur Tamang, Nirupa Tamang Dong and Rakesh Manandhar also went without medals in men’s kumite -60kg, women’s kumite -68kg and men’s kumite -55kg, respectively.

Despite the lack of medals this time, Dawa Gurung, general secretary of the Nepal Karate Federation, maintained that the athletes put up strong performances.

“Our athletes performed to the best of their abilities,” the general secretary said. “A few athletes, including Arika, won their preliminary bouts. In sports, whether national or international, becoming a champion requires more than just skill—everything has to go your way. I say with pride that the performance our athletes put up and how narrowly they lost, that defeat feels like a victory in itself. The players performed well. Perhaps, the managerial side fell short somewhere, and we take moral responsibility for that.”

Immediately following Tenzing’s match on Wednesday, the Nepali squad will travel to Tokyo to compete in the World Shito-Ryu Karate Championship. All karatekas who competed at the Asian Games will participate in the event.

title: Climate disasters are growing. So are cuts to programs that prepare for them - Bozeman Daily Chronicle
description: Climate disasters are growing. So are cuts to programs that prepare for them  Bozeman Daily Chronicle
publisher.title: Bozeman Daily Chronicle
full_article:
KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Sitting on the floor of a makeshift shelter for survivors of Nepal's deadly recent floods, Tenzin Dolma Ghale said she had nothing left but the clothes she was wearing. Her entire village and members of her family were washed away by the surge of water and debris that killed over 1,450 people and left more than 6,000 missing.

After speaking, she waved a hand and looked at the ground. “It’s all finished,” she said.

Ghale is among millions of people living with the deadly consequences of climate-related disasters. As such disasters intensify, international climate adaptation and disaster preparedness aid programs have been slashed, leaving countries facing billions of dollars in avoidable damage and dwindling recovery funds.





“The reality is that we need trillions of dollars every year, but developed countries have not met their obligation,” said Harjeet Singh, founding director of New Delhi-based Satat Sampada Climate Foundation.

Aid cuts weaken disaster monitoring in the Himalayas

The Trump administration’s abrupt cuts to U.S. foreign aid in 2025 eliminated or sharply curtailed programs serving millions of people worldwide, with devastating consequences for many communities. Reductions by other major donor countries deepened the funding crisis.

Among the programs shut was SERVIR-Hindu Kush Himalaya, a joint initiative of the U.S. Agency for International Development, NASA and the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, or ICIMOD.

Covering Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Nepal and Pakistan, the program used satellites and geospatial analysis for disaster risk reduction, water resources and land cover. It facilitated flood risk services, collaboration with the Nepal Red Cross Society on risk communication and more than 170 public data sets on glaciers, disasters and vulnerability.

Glacial and disaster preparedness experts praised the organization for its extensive research, cross-border coordination and support of local disaster reduction measures.

Before losing its funding due to USAID cuts, the program addressed mounting risks in a region where climate change has caused rapid glacier melt, shifting monsoons and increasingly frequent floods, landslides and glacial lake outburst floods, or GLOFs. Those changes endangered food, water and energy security for nearly 2 billion people living in or downstream of the region, according to ICIMOD.

Himalayan glaciers are losing mass 65% faster than they were a decade ago, according to a new report by global consultancy Systemiq, produced with ICIMOD. Yet only around 0.1% of the Himalaya’s estimated 40,000 glaciers are currently monitored in detail and on a sustained basis, the report said.

When funding for SERVIR-HKH ended, so did programs that monitored landslide forecasting, daily flooding, training programs and regional collaboration between countries.

With the program's loss, millions now face a heightened risk of GLOFs, which can release millions of cubic meters of water and debris in just a few hours.

In northern Pakistan, melting glaciers have created 3,044 glacial lakes, with over 30 identified as likely to result in such floods in areas where over 7 million people live, according to the United Nations Development Program.

Afghanistan also faces an increased threat of GLOFs, according to research published by the University of Lausanne in Switzerland.

In India — which was not part of the SERVIR-HKH program but borders all of the countries that were and is also home to over half the Himalayas — over 130 high-altitude lakes are at risk of flooding.

South Asia is already experiencing deadly climate-related disasters. The 2022 Pakistan floods killed more than 1,700 people and caused an estimated $40 billion in damage. Flooding in Nepal in 2025 killed nine people and caused millions of dollars in damage. Cloudbursts, landslides, flash floods and extreme rainfall have wreaked havoc in the Indian Himalayas, resulting in the death of over 12,000 people and damage exceeding billions of dollars in the last 15 years.

The region suffered economic losses of at least $7 billion in 2025 due to climate-driven extreme weather, according to the Emergency Events Database maintained by the University of Louvain, Belgium. This database itself is at risk of being shut down as a result of USAID funding cuts.

In a statement to The Associated Press, the U.S. State Department said that the U.S. supports Nepal’s flood warning capacity through programs with the World Meteorological Organization and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The department noted that SERVIR-HKH ended in January 2025 but that its tools remain active through ICIMOD.

The impact extends beyond communities hit directly. The Himalayan region is vital to national economies, with agriculture, industry, tourism and domestic use all dependent upon it.

Cuts to programs like SERVIR-HKH will have cascading effects for years, said Neha Rai, a climate finance expert at ICIMOD.

Rai likened the cuts to climate programs to abruptly halting funds for cancer research, which needs years of sustained research for success.

“Climate risk is also a generational challenge,” said Rai. “You need long-term observations, expertise, you need institutions that cannot simply be switched off and on as short-term priorities.”

Rai said cuts to cross-border programs have also impacted information sharing between governments, scientists and organizations across the region — a critical function in a region where what happens upstream directly affects countries downstream.

Climate finance shrinks as vulnerable countries face rising debt

These cuts are part of a larger trend. According to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, official development assistance from its Development Assistance Committee members, which includes the U.S., fell 23% in 2025 — the largest annual contraction on record. Traditionally large donors such as the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Japan and Canada have also announced massive reductions, reallocating funds to defense and other domestic priorities.

Global South countries spend approximately 225 times more in debt repayments than what they receive in grant-based climate finance, according to a recent report by the advocacy group, ActionAid International.

“There is a toxic relationship, in fact, between the climate crisis and the debt crisis,” said Teresa Andersen of ActionAid International.

She said countries take loans to recover from climate impacts but then cut investments in clean energy and preparations for future climate-related extreme weather to repay the loans.

The money being provided isn’t nearly enough, and climate often isn’t prioritized, said Richard Sherman, a board member of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, an international climate finance mechanism to assist developing countries vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change.

“There’s plenty of money if it goes to certain priorities, but for climate change right now, we’re witnessing a severe depreciation of the importance to act and make systems more resilient,” he said.

While disaster recovery funds still exist, they're also losing funding and aren’t equipped to handle the expected increase in disasters, he said.

“We’re not expecting developed countries to act as an ATM,” said Sherman. “But supporting vulnerable countries, helping them adapt and become more resilient means they’re less likely to suffer the kind of impacts we have right now.”

Arasu reported from Bengaluru, India.

title: Nepal and India agree to review trade treaty — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal and India agree to review trade treaty — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Nepal and India have agreed to review their bilateral trade treaty to address non-tariff barriers and Nepal's significant trade deficit with India. The way for the treaty review was opened by a meeting of the Nepal-India Intergovernmental Sub-Committee on Trade, Transit and Cooperation to Control Unauthorised Trade, held in New Delhi on September 16–17, Kathmandu Post reports.

Under the agreement, the sides are to convene a technical committee within six months. It will assess the scope of the current treaty and identify issues requiring changes in light of current global trade conditions.

Barriers to Nepalese exports

The treaty is to be reviewed every seven years, but over the past 17 years it has mostly been automatically extended without significant changes — in 2016 and 2023. The document provides for another automatic seven-year extension unless either side gives three months' notice of its intention to terminate it.

Experts point out that Nepalese exports to India are constrained by sanitary and phytosanitary requirements, technical barriers, complex procedures and high trade costs. Former commerce secretary Purushottam Ojha stressed the need to simplify documentation procedures, digitise trade, harmonise customs and border procedures, and resolve issues related to certificate accreditation.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

The current treaty provides duty-free and quota-free access for Nepalese goods to the Indian market, provided rules of origin are met. At the same time, quantitative restrictions apply to vegetable ghee, acrylic yarn, copper products and zinc oxide. Nepalese jute products have been subject to anti-dumping duties in India for almost a decade, although Nepalese producers deny selling their products at dumping prices.

Deficit and agricultural imports

India is Nepal's largest trading partner, accounting for more than 60% of the country's total trade. In the 2025–2026 fiscal year, bilateral merchandise trade exceeded 1.46 trillion Nepalese rupees. Nepal imported goods worth 1.21 trillion rupees from India and exported goods worth 258.65 billion rupees, resulting in a deficit of 951.95 billion rupees.

Experts link the imbalance, in particular, to imports of cheaper Indian agricultural products, with which Nepalese farmers cannot compete in terms of production costs. They propose excluding certain agricultural products from the mutual duty-free access regime, including cereals, rice, pulses, flour, livestock products, poultry, fish, honey and milk.

Refined soybean, palm and sunflower oil accounted for 57.59% of all Nepalese exports in the 2025–2026 fiscal year, or 148.96 billion rupees. Experts note that dependence on several commodity items calls the sustainability of export growth into question. The Nepalese side also plans to raise issues of trade in services, bilateral investment, paperless processing and cybersecurity during the treaty review.

The Trump administration’s abrupt cuts to U.S. foreign aid in 2025 eliminated or sharply curtailed programs serving millions of people worldwide, with devastating consequences for many communities. Reductions by other major donor countries deepened the funding crisis.

Among the programs shut was SERVIR-Hindu Kush Himalaya, a joint initiative of the U.S. Agency for International Development, NASA and the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, or ICIMOD.

Covering Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Nepal and Pakistan, the program used satellites and geospatial analysis for disaster risk reduction, water resources and land cover. It facilitated flood risk services, collaboration with the Nepal Red Cross Society on risk communication and more than 170 public data sets on glaciers, disasters and vulnerability.

Glacial and disaster preparedness experts praised the organization for its extensive research, cross-border coordination and support of local disaster reduction measures.

Before losing its funding due to USAID cuts, the program addressed mounting risks in a region where climate change has caused rapid glacier melt, shifting monsoons and increasingly frequent floods, landslides and glacial lake outburst floods, or GLOFs. Those changes endangered food, water and energy security for nearly 2 billion people living in or downstream of the region, according to ICIMOD.

Himalayan glaciers are losing mass 65% faster than they were a decade ago, according to a new report by global consultancy Systemiq, produced with ICIMOD. Yet only around 0.1% of the Himalaya’s estimated 40,000 glaciers are currently monitored in detail and on a sustained basis, the report said.

When funding for SERVIR-HKH ended, so did programs that monitored landslide forecasting, daily flooding, training programs and regional collaboration between countries.

With the program's loss, millions now face a heightened risk of GLOFs, which can release millions of cubic meters of water and debris in just a few hours.

In northern Pakistan, melting glaciers have created 3,044 glacial lakes, with over 30 identified as likely to result in such floods in areas where over 7 million people live, according to the United Nations Development Program.

Afghanistan also faces an increased threat of GLOFs, according to research published by the University of Lausanne in Switzerland.

In India — which was not part of the SERVIR-HKH program but borders all of the countries that were and is also home to over half the Himalayas — over 130 high-altitude lakes are at risk of flooding.

South Asia is already experiencing deadly climate-related disasters. The 2022 Pakistan floods killed more than 1,700 people and caused an estimated $40 billion in damage. Flooding in Nepal in 2025 killed nine people and caused millions of dollars in damage. Cloudbursts, landslides, flash floods and extreme rainfall have wreaked havoc in the Indian Himalayas, resulting in the death of over 12,000 people and damage exceeding billions of dollars in the last 15 years.

The region suffered economic losses of at least $7 billion in 2025 due to climate-driven extreme weather, according to the Emergency Events Database maintained by the University of Louvain, Belgium. This database itself is at risk of being shut down as a result of USAID funding cuts.

In a statement to The Associated Press, the U.S. State Department said that the U.S. supports Nepal’s flood warning capacity through programs with the World Meteorological Organization and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The department noted that SERVIR-HKH ended in January 2025 but that its tools remain active through ICIMOD.

The impact extends beyond communities hit directly. The Himalayan region is vital to national economies, with agriculture, industry, tourism and domestic use all dependent upon it.

Cuts to programs like SERVIR-HKH will have cascading effects for years, said Neha Rai, a climate finance expert at ICIMOD.

Rai likened the cuts to climate programs to abruptly halting funds for cancer research, which needs years of sustained research for success.

“Climate risk is also a generational challenge,” said Rai. “You need long-term observations, expertise, you need institutions that cannot simply be switched off and on as short-term priorities.”

Rai said cuts to cross-border programs have also impacted information sharing between governments, scientists and organizations across the region — a critical function in a region where what happens upstream directly affects countries downstream.

Climate finance shrinks as vulnerable countries face rising debt

These cuts are part of a larger trend. According to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, official development assistance from its Development Assistance Committee members, which includes the U.S., fell 23% in 2025 — the largest annual contraction on record. Traditionally large donors such as the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Japan and Canada have also announced massive reductions, reallocating funds to defense and other domestic priorities.

Global South countries spend approximately 225 times more in debt repayments than what they receive in grant-based climate finance, according to a recent report by the advocacy group, ActionAid International.

“There is a toxic relationship, in fact, between the climate crisis and the debt crisis,” said Teresa Andersen of ActionAid International.

She said countries take loans to recover from climate impacts but then cut investments in clean energy and preparations for future climate-related extreme weather to repay the loans.

The money being provided isn’t nearly enough, and climate often isn’t prioritized, said Richard Sherman, a board member of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, an international climate finance mechanism to assist developing countries vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change.

“There’s plenty of money if it goes to certain priorities, but for climate change right now, we’re witnessing a severe depreciation of the importance to act and make systems more resilient,” he said.

While disaster recovery funds still exist, they're also losing funding and aren’t equipped to handle the expected increase in disasters, he said.

“We’re not expecting developed countries to act as an ATM,” said Sherman. “But supporting vulnerable countries, helping them adapt and become more resilient means they’re less likely to suffer the kind of impacts we have right now.”

Arasu reported from Bengaluru, India.

title: US announces additional $31 million support for Nepal’s flood recovery - The Kathmandu Post
description: US announces additional $31 million support for Nepal’s flood recovery  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The United States has announced an additional $31 million in support for Nepal’s flood recovery efforts, including funds for permanent bridges, humanitarian assistance and US-made drones for future disaster recovery work.

US Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker made the announcement during a meeting with Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal in New York on Wednesday.

Hooker extended US sympathies to those affected by the devastating floods in Nepal, including the families of approximately 70 Americans who remain unaccounted for, according to a statement issued by the US Embassy in Kathmandu.

The United States plans to provide $10 million to build permanent, custom-built bridges in flood-affected areas. The bridges will be sourced from a US company and are intended to restore critical transportation infrastructure and strengthen regional connectivity.

The package also includes an additional $8 million for water, sanitation and hygiene, as well as shelter, protection, livelihoods and winterisation support for affected communities.

Another $13 million will be provided for US-made drones designed to support future disaster recovery efforts.

With the latest announcement, total US assistance to Nepal’s flood response and recovery efforts has risen to more than $36 million.

description: On Second Day in New York, Nepal’s Foreign Minister Focuses on Flood Recovery and Global South Cooperation  nepyork
publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
NEW YORK — Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal spent his second day in New York on Tuesday in a series of high-level diplomatic, bilateral and multilateral engagements as the 81st United Nations General Assembly high-level week got underway.

Khanal attended the welcoming ceremony for U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres before joining the opening session of the General Assembly’s high-level general debate at U.N. headquarters.

The general debate opened under the theme “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all.”

Prime Minister Balendra Shah is leading Nepal’s delegation to the General Assembly and is scheduled to address the Assembly on Thursday, Sept. 24.

Khanal’s second day in New York included meetings with officials from Slovakia, the Maldives, the United States and India, as well as a meeting that formally established diplomatic relations between Nepal and Grenada.

Khanal held a bilateral meeting with Slovak Foreign and European Affairs Minister Juraj Blanár, expressing appreciation to the Slovak government and people for their sympathy and solidarity following Nepal’s recent devastating climate disaster.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal meets Slovak Foreign and European Affairs Minister Juraj Blanár on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday. Photo by Rajan Kafle/NepYork.

The two ministers discussed ways to strengthen bilateral and multilateral cooperation. Their talks covered renewable energy, hydropower, tourism, technology and services, as well as early warning systems and cybersecurity. They also reaffirmed their commitment to multilateralism and closer cooperation at the United Nations.

Khanal also met Maldivian Foreign Minister Iruthisham Adam. He expressed appreciation to the Maldivian government and people for their sympathy, solidarity and humanitarian assistance following Nepal’s recent devastating floods.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal meets Maldivian Foreign Minister Iruthisham Adam on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday. Photo by Rajan Kafle/NepYork.

The two ministers discussed bilateral, regional and multilateral issues and ways to expand cooperation, including through exchanges of high-level visits and collaboration in tourism, employment and education. They also emphasized cooperation on climate change, development financing, sustainable development and other issues of common interest at the United Nations, the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation and other multilateral forums.

A key focus of Khanal’s U.S. engagement was Nepal’s flood recovery.

Khanal met U.S. Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker on the sidelines of the General Assembly. Hooker extended U.S. sympathies to those affected by the floods, including families of about 70 Americans who remained unaccounted for.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal meets U.S. Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker in New York on Tuesday. The two discussed Nepal-U.S. relations and U.S. support for Nepal’s flood recovery efforts. Photo by Rajan Kafle/NepYork.

During the meeting, Hooker announced plans to work with Congress to provide $10 million for permanent, custom-built bridges to restore transportation infrastructure in affected areas and improve regional connectivity. The bridges are expected to be sourced from a U.S. company.

The United States also plans to provide $8 million in additional assistance for water, sanitation and hygiene, shelter, protection, livelihoods and winterization support for affected communities. The State Department also plans to provide $13 million in U.S.-made drones to support future disaster recovery efforts.

The additional commitments would bring U.S. assistance for Nepal’s flood response and recovery to more than $36 million, according to the State Department.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal meets Dr. Joshua Walker, chief international affairs officer of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, in New York on Tuesday. Their discussions focused on investment opportunities, economic cooperation and business partnerships between Nepal and the United States. Photo by Rajan Kafle/NepYork.

Dr. Joshua Walker, chief international affairs officer at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, also paid a courtesy call on Khanal. Their discussions focused on investment opportunities, greater economic cooperation and strengthening business partnerships between Nepal and the United States. The official schedule had originally listed a meeting with Atul Keshap, the chamber’s senior vice president.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal meets Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday. Photo by Rajan Kafle/NepYork.

Khanal later met Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar on the sidelines of the General Assembly. Khanal expressed appreciation to the Indian government and people for their solidarity and immediate support following Nepal’s catastrophic floods.

The two ministers discussed issues of mutual interest and the need to further strengthen the longstanding ties between Nepal and India.

Khanal and Grenada’s Finance Minister Dennis Cornwall signed a joint communiqué formally establishing diplomatic relations between Nepal and Grenada during a ceremony at Nepal’s Permanent Mission to the U.N.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal and Grenada’s Finance Minister Dennis Cornwall sign a joint communiqué formally establishing diplomatic relations between Nepal and Grenada at Nepal’s Permanent Mission to the U.N. in New York on Tuesday. Photo by Rajan Kafle/NepYork.

Before the signing, the two ministers discussed efforts to accelerate progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals and address the effects of climate change. They also discussed opportunities to exchange experiences and best practices in tourism, education and other areas.

The agreement brings to 186 the number of countries with which Nepal has established diplomatic relations.

Khanal also addressed a high-level ministerial meeting of like-minded Global South countries and their friends organized by the Indian government on the sidelines of the General Assembly.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal addresses a high-level ministerial meeting of like-minded Global South countries and friends organized by India on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday. Photo by Rajan Kafle/NepYork.

He highlighted the transformative potential of the Global South and the importance of giving developing countries a stronger voice in global decision-making. Khanal called for greater collective action, stronger South-South cooperation and a more equitable and representative global governance system.

“By empowering the Global South, we revitalize multilateralism itself,” Khanal said.

Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai separately took part in a high-level discussion at U.N. headquarters titled “Beyond 2030: Renewing the Global Commitment to End Poverty in All its Dimensions,” organized by Bhutan’s Permanent Mission.

Rai said poverty is not only a lack of income but also a denial of basic capabilities, security and human agency. He called for a multidimensional approach to poverty eradication and highlighted Nepal’s progress as well as its continuing challenges.

Nepal’s Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai addresses a high-level discussion on “Beyond 2030: Renewing the Global Commitment to End Poverty in All its Dimensions” at U.N. headquarters in New York on Tuesday. Photo by Rajan Kafle/NepYork.

Rai also highlighted the disproportionate effects of the accelerating climate crisis, including the loss of lives and damage to critical infrastructure during Nepal’s recent climate disaster. He called for climate-resilient development, climate justice, greater access to financing and technology, and faster implementation of global development commitments, including the 2030 Agenda and the Pact for the Future.

Nepal’s Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai meets Dulguun Damdin-Od, executive director of the International Think Tank for Landlocked Developing Countries, in New York on Tuesday.

Rai separately met Dulguun Damdin-Od, executive director of the International Think Tank for Landlocked Developing Countries. Their discussions covered connectivity, aviation, climate issues, critical minerals, youth engagement and the Awaza Programme of Action.

Khanal also met Jagan Chapagain, secretary general of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, at Nepal’s Permanent Mission, according to the official schedule.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal meets Jagan Chapagain, secretary general of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, in New York on Tuesday. Photo by Rajan Kafle/NepYork.

Khanal visited the Consulate General of Nepal in New York for a briefing and took part in an interview during the afternoon.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal visits the Consulate General of Nepal in New York for a briefing during his second day of engagements on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly. Photo by Rajan Kafle/NepYork.

Khanal later attended a reception hosted by the president of the United States, concluding his second day of engagements in New York.

title: Khanal holds multiple diplomatic meetings in New York as Nepal establishes ties with Grenada - The Kathmandu Post
description: Khanal holds multiple diplomatic meetings in New York as Nepal establishes ties with Grenada  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal attended the opening of the General Debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at the UN Headquarters in New York on Tuesday as part of a series of diplomatic engagements.

The General Debate was held under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All”.

The debate was opened by General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman, followed by an address by UN Secretary-General António Guterres and statements by heads of delegations of UN member states.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who is leading the Nepali delegation, is scheduled to address the General Assembly on September 24.

Earlier in the afternoon, Khanal addressed a High-Level Ministerial Meeting of Like-Minded Global South Countries and Friends, convened by the Government of India under the theme “Navigating Together Towards a Brighter Future–The Compelling Case for an Empowered Global South”.

Khanal stressed the importance of solidarity, cooperation and collective action among Global South countries in addressing shared global challenges and advancing common priorities.

He also highlighted the transformative potential of the Global South and called for collective resolve, stronger South-South cooperation and a more equitable and representative global governance architecture.

In a separate bilateral meeting with Indian External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, Khanal expressed appreciation to the government and people of India for their solidarity and immediate critical support following the recent catastrophic floods in Nepal.

The two ministers also discussed matters of common interest and underscored the need to enhance development cooperation while further strengthening the close and longstanding ties between Nepal and India.

Khanal also held bilateral meetings with Slovak Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Juraj Blanár and Maldivian Foreign Minister Iruthisham Adam.

They exchanged views on further consolidating bilateral relations and cooperation in areas of mutual interest, including at the United Nations.

US Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker also called on Khanal.

According to the Permanent Mission of Nepal to the United Nations, they discussed several issues of common interest, including deepening Nepal-US relations, relief and reconstruction following the recent climate-induced Bhotekoshi floods, and continued US support for Nepal’s recovery efforts.

Khanal also met Atul Keshap, senior vice-president of the US Chamber of Commerce, to discuss expanding investment opportunities, enhancing economic ties and strengthening business partnerships between Nepal and the United States.

Meanwhile, Khanal and Dennis Cornwall, Minister for Finance of Grenada, signed a Joint Communiqué formally establishing diplomatic relations between Nepal and Grenada.

Before the brief signing ceremony at the Nepal Mission, the two ministers exchanged views on a range of issues of mutual interest.

They underscored the importance of accelerating progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals, addressing the impacts of climate change, and sharing best practices in tourism, education and other areas of mutual benefit.

With the establishment of diplomatic relations with Grenada, Nepal’s diplomatic outreach has expanded to 186 countries, according to the Permanent Mission of Nepal to the United Nations.

In the evening, Khanal attended a reception hosted by US President Donald J. Trump in honour of heads of delegations of UN member states participating in the 81st session of the General Assembly.

Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai addressed the High-Level Discussion on “Beyond 2030: Renewing the Global Commitment to End Poverty in All its Dimensions”.

Rai called for climate-resilient development, climate justice, efforts to close financing and technology gaps, and tangible progress on global development commitments, including the 2030 Agenda and the Pact for the Future.

Rai also held a meeting with Dulguun Damdin-Od, executive director of the International Think Tank for Landlocked Developing Countries.

They discussed the organisation’s work to advance the shared interests of landlocked developing countries, including connectivity and aviation, climate change, critical minerals, youth engagement and effective implementation of the Awaza Programme of Action.

title: Georgia Couple Reflects on Surviving Deadly Nepal Flood: ‘I Don’t Have an Answer’ - Yahoo
description: Georgia Couple Reflects on Surviving Deadly Nepal Flood: ‘I Don’t Have an Answer’  Yahoo
publisher.title: Yahoo
full_article:
NEED TO KNOW

Mita and Hemant Parikh survived Nepal's deadly August floods after an unplanned excursion to Mount Everest, they told CBS Atlanta in a new interview on Tuesday, Sept. 22

Their travel group, including seven guides, remains missing after the floods devastated the region

The couple had been planning the sacred pilgrimage to Mount Kailash for 15 years before the tragedy struck

A Georgia couple is discussing their experience with traveling to Nepal during fatal flooding in August.

Mita and Hemant Parikh, residents of Suwanee, Ga., were traveling to Mount Kailash in the Himalayan range in Tibet, a sacred site in Hinduism, according to CBS Atlanta. The couple were part of a group of 47 travelers composed of families from Australia, the U.S., and more. The group was led by seven guides.

Several families and all of the guides are currently missing, the outlet reported. A brief excursion to Lhasa and Everest Base Camp, off the travel group's path, is ultimately what saved the Parikhs' lives.

"That's what we talk to each other every single day," Mita told the outlet. "Why did we decide this way?"

The couple told the local news station they had been planning this pilgrimage for 15 years.

"Everybody has a bucket list, but this bucket list, you don't choose it," Mita said, per the outlet. "God chooses for you."

The couple recounted the surreal moment they made the life-saving decision to change their itinerary to see Mount Everest.

"Usually we argue, or tickets are expensive — no, let's not go," Mita recalled to CBS Atlanta. "But I don't know why we both agreed."

Hemant had pushed for the excursion in hopes of catching a glimpse of the legendary mountain.

"Mount Everest is the highest peak in the world," he told the outlet. "And I said, at least, I cannot climb, but I can go and see from a distance."

Credit: Prabin RANABHAT / AFP via Getty

After viewing the mountain, the couple planned to return to the group with their separate guide who brought them to the viewing point — only to discover that the hotel they had been staying at was entirely washed away from the floods, and they were unable to reach anyone in their travel group.

"As soon as I close my eyes, I see Kailash, and I see the people," Mita told CBS Atlanta. "I don't know what happened."

"I ask myself why?" Hemant said of questioning how he and his wife became potentially the group's sole survivors. "And I don't have an answer."

"That's what keeps me awake," Mita added. "Why? Why God chose us to live. So there has to be some purpose, right?"

The flooding has caused widespread devastation to Nepal's infrastructure, and at least 1,400 people have died.

More than 6,000 people remain missing, according to the Associated Press. Of those missing, at least 85 are U.S. citizens, per Politico.
